title: How to Assess Your Accountant’s Actual Payroll Scope
summary: Most growth-stage companies do not choose to run payroll through their accountant. They inherit the arrangement. The CPA firm that filed the first year of business taxes started reconciling payroll entries, then started answering payroll questions, and at some point…
body_markdown:
Most growth-stage companies do not choose to run payroll through their accountant. They inherit the arrangement. The CPA firm that filed the first year of business taxes started reconciling payroll entries, then started answering payroll questions, and at some point "our accountant handles payroll" became an assumption nobody tested. That assumption holds fine at five employees on a single pay schedule in one state. It becomes a liability once headcount grows, states multiply, and the tasks nobody explicitly assigned start missing deadlines.


This guide is a single procedure: assess exactly what your current or prospective accountant will and will not do for payroll, in writing, before you rely on it. It is built for the owner, CFO, or HR leader at a company roughly 10 to 250 employees who needs to know whether the accountant relationship covers what the business actually needs, or only part of it. By the end, you will have a documented scope map that names every payroll task, marks it covered or uncovered, and assigns liability for errors, so nothing is running on assumption when the next payroll cycle or filing deadline arrives.


Use this before assuming an accountant covers payroll processing, at the start of a new engagement, during an annual engagement review, or any time a missed deadline or unexpected notice suggests the scope was never actually confirmed.


## What you need before you start


- Your current or prospective accountant's engagement letter or service agreement
- A working list of your business's payroll tasks (processing, tax filings, reconciliation, year-end)
- At least one scheduled call or meeting with the accountant or firm contact
- Current headcount, pay schedule count, and the list of states where you have employees
- An internal owner (you, your controller, or your HR lead) who will hold the finished scope map


## Step 1. Build a complete inventory of your payroll tasks


Before you can assess coverage, you need the full list of what payroll actually requires rather than the shorthand version. Write down every task your business needs performed on a recurring basis: wage calculation, payment issuance (direct deposit or checks), tax withholding calculation, quarterly federal payroll tax filing, state withholding and unemployment filings, new-hire reporting, garnishment processing, benefits deduction management, payroll journal entry posting, monthly reconciliation, W-2 and 1099 preparation, and multi-state registration if you have or plan to have employees in more than one state. Most owners can name three or four of these without prompting. The rest are the ones that quietly fall into a gap.


## Step 2. Pull the engagement letter and read it before the meeting


Do this before you talk to anyone. Most standard bookkeeping and tax engagement letters explicitly exclude payroll processing, and many limit the accountant's role to recording and reconciling entries after payroll has already run somewhere else. Look for the specific language used: "payroll processing," "payroll tax filing," and "payroll accounting" are three different things, and a letter that mentions one does not confirm the others. If the letter is silent on payroll entirely, treat that as a gap to raise directly rather than an implied yes.


## Step 3. Request a written scope map sorted into three categories


Ask your accountant, in writing, to map every task from your Step 1 list into one of three categories: included in the current engagement, available as a paid add-on, or not offered at all. Do this before the meeting so the conversation is a review of their answers instead of a live improvisation. A written response also becomes the record you rely on later if a task turns out to be uncovered. Verbal assurances during a phone call are not a substitute; get the categorization in an email or a revised letter.


## Step 4. Separate payroll accounting from payroll processing


This is the distinction most scope confusion comes from, and it is worth understanding in concrete terms before you review the accountant's answers. Payroll accounting typically means the accountant records payroll journal entries after the fact, reconciles payroll register totals against the general ledger, and prepares year-end tax documents from data someone else generated. Payroll processing means someone is calculating gross wages, applying withholdings, issuing the actual payment, and filing the associated tax returns on a live schedule. Tax strategy and advisory work, such as year-end planning, entity structure guidance, or estimated tax planning for owners, is a third, separate category again. An accountant who says they "handle payroll" may mean any one of these three things. Get them to specify which.


## Step 5. Ask the scope questions directly, not generally


"Do you handle payroll?" is not a useful question because the honest answer is almost always some version of yes. Ask instead:


- "Do you calculate and issue paychecks, or only record them after they've been run through a processor?"
- "Who initiates the actual tax deposit and files the return, you or a separate payroll system?"
- "If we hire in a new state, do you handle the withholding and unemployment tax registration, or is that our responsibility?"
- "If a state or federal agency sends a notice about our payroll taxes, who receives it, and who is responsible for responding?"
- "What is your turnaround time on W-2 and 1099 preparation relative to your other tax season work?"


These questions surface the operational reality that a general "we handle payroll" answer tends to obscure.


## Step 6. Flag the gap tasks that carry compliance deadlines


Once you have the accountant's category-by-category answers, isolate anything marked "not offered" or "add-on" and check it against your original task list. Pay particular attention to tasks that carry a hard compliance deadline rather than an internal one, because these are the ones most likely to be missed silently rather than flagged as a problem. In practice, the gap tasks that recur most often for growth-stage companies are:


- **Multi-state registration.** Before you run payroll for an employee in a new state, your business generally needs active withholding and unemployment tax accounts in that state. Many accounting engagements do not include monitoring for this, which means it falls through unless someone owns it explicitly.
- **Quarterly federal payroll tax filing (Form 941).** This is the employer's quarterly federal tax return covering withheld income and FICA taxes. Bookkeeping-only engagements frequently exclude the associated tax deposit and filing cycle, even when the accountant is recording the related journal entries.
- **New-hire reporting.** Most states require employers to report newly hired employees to a state agency within a defined window after hire. This is rarely part of a standard tax engagement and is easy to miss because it does not resemble accounting work.
- **W-2 and 1099 preparation timing.** Many accountants do prepare these, but often on their own tax-season schedule rather than the timeline your business, employees, or benefits vendors actually need them on. Confirm turnaround expectations as well as whether the task is covered at all.
- **State unemployment insurance filings.** Distinct from federal filings and easy to assume is bundled with "payroll taxes" generally when it is often a separate filing obligation entirely.


## Step 7. Get liability allocation in writing for every category


For each task, confirm in writing who is responsible if it is done wrong or missed: the accountant, your business, or a shared arrangement. Accountants rarely indemnify clients for processing errors as a standard part of a bookkeeping engagement, and as the employer, your business is typically the default party an agency will hold accountable regardless of who was supposed to perform the task. Do not treat this step as adversarial. It is a normal, professional request, and a firm that resists documenting it in writing is itself useful information about how the relationship will handle a real problem.


## Step 8. Score the coverage against your actual complexity


A scope map is only useful if you evaluate it against where your business actually is, not where it was when the accountant relationship started. Score the coverage against three variables: current headcount, the number of distinct pay schedules you run, and your state footprint. A scope that was sufficient at 12 employees on one payroll schedule in one state is frequently insufficient at 60 employees across three states with hourly and salaried pay cycles running in parallel. If any gap task from Step 6 intersects with a variable that has grown since the engagement started, treat the scope as structurally incomplete rather than adequate with exceptions.


## Step 9. Document the scope map and set a review trigger


Put the finished scope map, covered tasks, gap tasks, and liability allocation, into a single document and share it with your finance and HR leads so ownership is unambiguous before the next payroll cycle. Set a specific trigger for reassessment rather than leaving the review open-ended: a defined headcount threshold, expansion into a new state, or a missed filing in the past twelve months are all reasonable triggers. If you're still working out who inside your company should own the payroll relationship day to day once the scope is clear, whether that lands with your CFO, your HR lead, or someone else, that internal ownership question is addressed in[who handles payroll, HR, or finance for growth-stage companies](https://www.asuresoftware.com/who-handles-payroll-hr-or-finance-answers-for-growth-stage-companies/) .


## What to do once the scope gap is identified


If your scope map from Step 9 shows every task covered and liability clearly allocated, you may not need to change anything. That outcome is common at the smaller end of this range and is a legitimate result of the exercise, one that simply found nothing worth flagging.


If the map shows gap tasks, particularly ones tied to a compliance deadline, you have two general ways to fill them without restructuring your entire accountant relationship. AsureCentral is a connected payroll and HR platform that lets your team run the excluded tasks yourselves, including wage calculation, payment issuance, and tax filing, inside one system rather than reconstructing them across spreadsheets and separate logins. AsureWorks takes the opposite approach to the same problem: Asure specialists process payroll, handle the tax filing and reporting your accountant does not cover, and manage the related HR documentation directly, while your business remains the employer of record throughout. AsureWorks is not a PEO and does not involve co-employment; you keep your existing benefits, broker, and retirement program choices, and Asure takes over execution of the specific tasks your scope map identified as uncovered.


A useful way to think about the choice: a 40-employee professional services firm that just opened a second state office might keep tax strategy and entity planning with its CPA, then move quarterly filings, new-hire reporting, and multi-state registration onto AsureCentral so the team runs those tasks directly inside one system instead of tracking them by hand. A company at similar size with no internal payroll administrator might instead hand those same gap tasks to AsureWorks specialists rather than build the internal capacity to run them.


Deciding between running the gap tasks yourself and having them handled for you is a separate decision from the scope assessment itself, and it deserves its own evaluation of cost, internal capacity, and how much of the work you want to keep in-house. ## Frequently asked questions


**Do accountants typically handle payroll, or is it a separate service?** Most accountants treat payroll as a separate, optional service rather than a default part of a bookkeeping or tax engagement. Some CPA firms do offer full payroll processing, but many limit their role to payroll accounting, recording entries and reconciling accounts, rather than running payroll itself. Confirm scope explicitly rather than assuming coverage.


**What payroll tasks will an accountant actually take on for a growing business?** Accountants commonly handle payroll journal entries, reconciliation, and year-end tax document preparation. Fewer routinely handle live payroll processing, meaning calculating wages, issuing payments, and filing quarterly tax returns on an ongoing schedule. Scope varies firm to firm, which is exactly why a written task list matters more than a general description of services.


**Who is liable for payroll tax errors, the business, the accountant, or a payroll provider?** Liability depends on the specific service agreements in place. As the employer, your business is generally the default party an agency holds accountable for payroll tax errors. Accountants rarely indemnify clients for processing mistakes as standard practice. Some managed payroll providers do assume defined liability for errors within their scope. Confirm the allocation in writing with every party involved in your payroll operation, including the one you already assume is responsible.
